messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 62
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bank Teller
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 58

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Known People: Related people, Stress: Stress, Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
  Negative Appraisals: Inadequacy: I am inadequate, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Robert had always considered his hands to be steady. For forty years as a bank teller, they had counted currency with a crisp, confident rhythm. They had built bookshelves, repaired leaky faucets, and, most importantly, they had held his grandson. That was the memory that now tormented him. The accident had happened six months ago, on a Saturday that was supposed to be perfect. He was at his son’s house, helping to build a small deck in the backyard. The circular saw whined in the afternoon sun, and Robert was focused, measuring a cut. He never heard his grandson, Leo, run up behind him. The first thing he felt was the small, enthusiastic bump against his back, a child’s hug in motion. Startled, Robert lurched, and the saw kicked. The next few seconds unfolded in a silent, horrifying slow motion in his mind: the high-pitched scream, the impossible splash of red on Leo’s jacket, the sight of his own hands, the ones that were supposed to be steady, covered in his grandson’s blood.

Now, those hands tremble. At work, Robert positions his chair tightly against the back of his teller station, a small fortress so that no one can approach from behind. An unexpected touch is unbearable. Last week, a regular customer, Mrs. Gable, reached over the counter to tap his hand affectionately, and he flinched so violently he knocked over his coin tray. The cascade of metal on the floor sounded like a siren in his ears. In that moment, he wasn't in the bank; he was back in the yard, the smell of sawdust and copper in the air. A fragment of the memory, Leo's face contorted in pain, flashed behind his eyes and was gone, leaving him breathless and dizzy. When he remembers the event, the same sickening terror he felt in that instant washes over him, a cold wave that starts in his stomach and leaves him shaking. Immediately following the fear is a crushing, suffocating guilt. He believes he is fundamentally inadequate, a man who failed in his most basic duty to protect his family.

His life has shrunk into a series of defensive maneuvers. He avoids his son’s calls, the cheerful ringtone of his phone now a source of dread. He hasn’t seen Leo since the boy came home from the hospital, his arm wrapped in thick bandages. The thought of seeing the scar, a permanent testament to his failure, is more than he can stand. His son and daughter-in-law insist they don’t blame him, that it was a terrible accident, but their words are meaningless to him. How could they not blame him? He blames himself enough for everyone. This conviction, that his reactions prove he is a lousy coper, has become a core belief. A real man, he thinks, would have faced his family, would have been there for his grandson. Instead, he hides.

The world outside his carefully controlled teller station feels fraught with peril. He is constantly on guard, his body rigid with a tension that never subsides. Even at home, in his favourite armchair, he cannot relax. While his wife watches television, he finds himself scanning the room, listening to the house settle, his heart pounding at every floorboard creak. Sleep offers no escape. He lies awake for hours, certain that he must remain alert, though he doesn't know for what. He feels as though some unseen threat is perpetually waiting, and if he lets his guard down, it will strike. He has come to believe that the cheerful, easygoing man his wife married is gone forever, replaced by this hollow, fearful shell. He feels he has been permanently changed for the worse, and this new version of himself is all he has left. It was after he found himself awake for the third straight night, staring at the ceiling and replaying the saw's screech in his mind, that his wife found him weeping in the kitchen. The next morning, she made the appointment. Robert agreed to come, not with hope, but with a profound fear that the therapist would only confirm what he already knew: that he was broken beyond repair.
